title: "Free coins" scams in games
intro: Lots of games sell coins, gems or skins. Scammers know everyone wants them for free.
They promise free coins, and in return they ask for a password, a code sent by text, an app download or a gift card code.
The rule: real coins only come from inside the game itself or its official store, and never in exchange for a password.

game.prompt: Sort each offer: safe or a scam?
game.practiceNotice: These are practice offers we made up for this game. They are not real.

items.text: A website promises 10,000 coins if you log in with your game username and password
items.explain: A random site asking for your password wants to steal your account.

items.text: The game itself gives you 50 coins for finishing a level
items.explain: Rewards inside the game, for something you did, are the normal way to get coins.

items.text: A player in chat: give me your coins and I'll give you back double
items.explain: "Give me yours and I'll double them" is an old trick. The coins never come back.

items.text: Your parents buy coins in the game's official store
items.explain: Buying with your parents in the official store is the safe way.

items.text: A video tells you to download a "coin generator" app
items.explain: Coin generators don't exist. Apps like that can be a virus or steal your account.

items.text: An event inside the game gives a prize to everyone who takes part
items.explain: Events inside the game itself are safe, and you don't have to give any details.

items.text: A message: send the code from a gift card and get ten times the coins
items.explain: Anyone asking for a gift card code wants the money. No official game asks for that.

quiz.question: An offer sounds too good to be true. What does that usually mean?
options: You should hurry before it runs out
quiz.explain: When something sounds too good, that's the sign to stop and check with a grown-up.

quiz.question: Someone asks for your password so they can add coins. What do you do?
options: Don't give it, and tell a parent
quiz.explain: Nobody needs your password to give you coins. Whoever asks for it wants to steal.

quiz.question: Where do real coins come from?
options: Sites that ask you to log in
The game itself or its official store
quiz.explain: Only the game itself and its official store give real coins.

summary: Free coins in exchange for a password, a code or a download are a scam. Real coins only come from the game or its official store, and you tell a parent about any strange offer.
